title: OpenAI ships GPT-6 Astra — the first model rated 'Critical' for cyber capability
subtitle: Astra scored a perfect 100 on ExploitBench and autonomously found two live V8 zero-days in evals, crossing OpenAI's Preparedness Framework threshold that triggers deployment restrictions.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra on September 3, priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens on the standard API with a 1.05M context window. The release rolls out first to Daybreak program companies, then to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers, then to the OpenAI API and AWS. An optional Fast mode is available at 2x price for 2.5x speed.

The disclosure that matters is the safety card. OpenAI classified Astra as 'Critical' for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework — the first model to cross that threshold — after the model scored a perfect 100 on ExploitBench (up from 78.5 for GPT-5.6 Sol) and autonomously discovered and exploited two previously unknown high-severity V8 zero-days during evaluation. Both were disclosed to maintainers. The 'Critical' label triggers additional restrictions: Astra will refuse to write proof-of-concept exploits, and full cyber capabilities are gated behind Daybreak for Frontline Defenders.

This is the point where OpenAI's own governance framework meets a shipped product. Astra is not the first frontier model to demonstrate offensive cyber capability in a controlled test, but it is the first one that the developer has publicly acknowledged clears the threshold their own policy said would require staged deployment and restricted access. That precedent will now be cited by every other frontier lab writing similar policies — and by every regulator arguing they need visibility into what those evals actually measure.

For learners: the takeaway is that a model's headline capability numbers and its access policy are now inseparable. A model rated 'Critical' does not mean it is broken or dangerous by default — it means the developer has decided some capabilities cost more to open than to hold. Reading the Preparedness Framework and the safety overview alongside the benchmark tables is a better way to understand what a frontier release actually is than reading either alone.
